p.src: What is a quantum field, and how is it related to particles? The basic mathematical tool is the harmonic oscillator. A field contains many possible modes of oscillation, and quantizing the field amounts to putting together one quantum harmonic oscillator for each mode. The construction is easiest to see first in a finite periodic space, where the allowed modes form a discrete list.

p.src: Take one spatial coordinate $x$ and identify points separated by a distance $L$. One can picture the space as a circle of circumference $L$. This is a useful finite-volume trick. On a finite interval with endpoints, a traveling wave reflects from the ends. On a periodic interval it can continue in either direction without reflection. Translation symmetry, and therefore momentum conservation, is retained while the complications of infinite volume are temporarily removed.

p.src:
A plane wave has the form $e^{ikx}.$ After one trip around the circle it must return to its original value. Since the wave equals $1$ at $x=0$, periodicity requires $e^{ikL}=1.$ Why does an integer multiple of $2\pi$ solve this condition? Euler’s formula gives $\begin{aligned}e^{i2\pi n}
&=\cos(2\pi n)+i\sin(2\pi n)\\
&=1,
\qquad n\in\mathbb Z.\end{aligned}$ The cosine is $1$ and the sine is $0$ after any whole number of cycles. Consequently, $kL=2\pi n,
\qquad
k=\frac{2\pi n}{L},
\qquad n\in\mathbb Z.$ The quantity $k$ is the wave number. The integer $n$ labels an allowed wave number; it is not yet counting particles.

p.src: A quantum state is a vector, or linear element. State vectors can be added and multiplied by numbers, and operators act on them to produce other state vectors. Observable real quantities are represented by Hermitian operators. These elementary facts matter here because both the many-particle state and the field will be built from linear combinations and operators.

p.src:
Each momentum mode is a harmonic oscillator. It therefore has a raising operator and a lowering operator. The notation written initially as $a^{+}(k)$ and $a^{-}(k)$ will be written as $a^\dagger(k)$ and $a(k)$. Their actions are $\begin{aligned}a^\dagger(k)\big|\ldots,n(k),\ldots\big\rangle
&=
\sqrt{n(k)+1}\notag\\
&\quad{}\times
\big|\ldots,n(k)+1,\ldots\big\rangle,
\\
a(k)\big|\ldots,n(k),\ldots\big\rangle
&=
\sqrt{n(k)}\,
\big|\ldots,n(k)-1,\ldots\big\rangle.\end{aligned}$ The operator $a^\dagger(k)$ goes to the slot belonging to $k$, raises that occupation by one, and multiplies the state by $\sqrt{n(k)+1}$. The operator $a(k)$ lowers the same slot and supplies $\sqrt{n(k)}$. There is one such pair for every allowed momentum.

p.src: The complex field has a real and an imaginary part. Its complex conjugate reverses the sign of the imaginary part, and $e^{ikx}$ becomes $e^{-ikx}$. Specifying all the coefficients $\alpha(k)$ specifies the classical field. There is no need to specify $\alpha^*(k)$ independently once $\alpha(k)$ is known, but the real and imaginary parts of each coefficient are separate real quantities. They can be measured as the amplitudes of the corresponding Fourier components. In this sense a complex coefficient packages two classical observables.

Reversing every sign consistently would describe the same construction.)

p.src:
First consider a process that does not change the number of particles. Suppose the only particle initially present has momentum $k_7$. In occupation-number notation its state has a $1$ in the seventh slot and zeros everywhere else: $|k_7\rangle
=
|\ldots,0,\underset{k_7}{1},0,\ldots\rangle.$ A scattering process changes its momentum from $k_7$ to $k_9$. The operator that makes exactly this change is $a^\dagger(k_9)a(k_7).$ The rightmost operator acts first: it removes the particle in the $k_7$ slot. The left operator then creates a particle in the $k_9$ slot.

Let us carry out both steps. Annihilation gives $\begin{aligned}a(k_7)|k_7\rangle
&=
\sqrt{1}\,|\ldots,0,0,0,\ldots\rangle\\
&=|0\rangle.\end{aligned}$ The all-zero state is the vacuum. It is the state with no particles, and in this simple collection of oscillators it is also the ground state. Creation in the empty $k_9$ mode then gives $a^\dagger(k_9)|0\rangle
=\sqrt{0+1}\,|k_9\rangle
=|k_9\rangle.$ Consequently, $a^\dagger(k_9)a(k_7)|k_7\rangle=|k_9\rangle.$ Slot by slot, the sole $1$ has simply moved from the seventh momentum mode to the ninth. Because no occupation ever exceeded one, both square-root factors were equal to one. They will become important as soon as an already occupied mode is involved.

This one-to-one process could also be described in ordinary single-particle quantum mechanics: one particle changes its momentum. The occupation-number language becomes indispensable when particle number can change. For example, $a^\dagger(k_9)a^\dagger(k_{16})a(k_7)|k_7\rangle
=|k_9,k_{16}\rangle$ describes the mathematical change from one incoming particle in mode $k_7$ to two outgoing particles, one in $k_9$ and one in $k_{16}$. A target may absorb the incoming particle, emit the two outgoing particles, and take up whatever recoil is required. Such a process cannot be represented in a Hilbert space restricted to one particle, but it fits naturally in a state space whose occupation numbers can vary. The operator expression is not by itself a law of nature; it is the language in which a number-changing law can be written.

The field operator $\Psi^\dagger(x)$ creates the coherent superposition of allowed momentum states that is formally localized at $x$.

Now suppose there is already one photon in mode $\ell$. Acting with the same local creation field gives two kinds of terms: $\Psi^\dagger(x)|\ell\rangle

For every momentum mode there are creation and annihilation operators. Their algebra is $\begin{aligned}[a^\dagger(k),a^\dagger(\ell)]&=0,\\
[a(k),a(\ell)]&=0,\\
[a(k),a^\dagger(\ell)]&=\delta_{k\ell}.\end{aligned}$ Here $[A,B]=AB-BA,$ and the Kronecker delta is $\delta_{k\ell}=
\begin{cases}
1,&k=\ell,\\
0,&k\ne\ell.
\end{cases}$ Creation operators commute for equal or unequal momenta, as do annihilation operators. A mixed pair commutes for different momenta; for the same momentum it has the familiar single-oscillator commutator.

Consider now the operator $\int_0^L dx\,\Psi^\dagger(x)\Psi(x).$ Instead of naming it in advance, work it out. Substitution of the Fourier expansions gives $\begin{aligned}\int_0^L dx\,\Psi^\dagger(x)\Psi(x)
&=
\sum_{k,\ell}a^\dagger(k)a(\ell)
\int_0^L dx\,e^{-ikx}e^{i\ell x}
\\
&=
\sum_{k,\ell}a^\dagger(k)a(\ell)
\int_0^L dx\,e^{i(\ell-k)x}.\end{aligned}$ If $k=\ell$, the exponential is $1$ and the integral is $L$. If $k\ne\ell$, an integer number of sine and cosine cycles is integrated around the circle; positive and negative parts cancel. Thus $\int_0^L dx\,e^{i(\ell-k)x}=L\delta_{k\ell}.$ The double sum collapses to $\int_0^L dx\,\Psi^\dagger(x)\Psi(x)
=L\sum_k a^\dagger(k)a(k).$ For each mode, $a^\dagger(k)a(k)=N_k$ is the occupation-number operator. Summing it counts all particles: $N=\sum_k N_k=\sum_k a^\dagger(k)a(k).$ With the present Fourier normalization, $N=\frac{1}{L}\int_0^L dx\,
\Psi^\dagger(x)\Psi(x).$ Other conventions put factors such as $1/\sqrt{L}$ into the Fourier expansion and remove the explicit $1/L$ here. In the convention being used, the local number-density operator is $\rho(x)=\frac{1}{L}\Psi^\dagger(x)\Psi(x),
\qquad
\int_0^L dx\,\rho(x)=N.$ Thus $\Psi^\dagger(x)\Psi(x)$ is proportional to particle density. Calling it the number of particles at one mathematical point is misleading; density is the appropriate local notion.

p.src:
A complex field operator is not itself a single Hermitian observable. Its two Hermitian components are $\Psi_1(x)=\frac{\Psi(x)+\Psi^\dagger(x)}{2},
\quad
\Psi_2(x)=\frac{\Psi(x)-\Psi^\dagger(x)}{2i}.$ They are the quantum analogs of the real and imaginary parts of a classical field. They do not commute, so both cannot be measured simultaneously with arbitrary precision. This is the field version of the uncertainty between the conjugate variables of a harmonic oscillator.

p.src: When, then, can the field behave like a classical wave? Consider one highly excited momentum mode $k$. Its number operator is $a^\dagger(k)a(k)=N_k.$ Suppose the state has a large mean occupation, $\langle N_k\rangle=n_k\gg 1$. The scale available to a macroscopic oscillator amplitude is then of order $\sqrt{n_k}$. Meanwhile, the right-hand side of $[a(k),a^\dagger(k)]=1$ remains fixed. The commutator never vanishes, but at large occupation its effects can be small compared with the squared scale of the excitation. Large occupation supplies the scale needed for a classical limit, but it is not sufficient by itself. The state must also be appropriately phase coherent, so that the uncertainties of the two quadratures are small compared with the macroscopic field amplitude. (This qualifies the large-occupation heuristic. A number eigenstate has $\langle a(k)\rangle=0$, no definite phase, and quadrature fluctuations of order $\sqrt{n_k}$; it is not by itself a classical wave.)

p.src: For an electromagnetic field, large occupation means many photons. In an appropriately phase-coherent state with many photons in the relevant modes, the measurable field components behave approximately like an ordinary classical electromagnetic wave. With only a few photons, the discreteness of the quanta is visible and the classical wave description fails. A quantum field remains an operator in both regimes; what changes is the relative importance of its quantum fluctuations.

A particle that crosses the right edge reappears at the corresponding point on the left. If it crosses the top, it reappears at the corresponding point on the bottom. A periodic field obeys $\begin{aligned}\Psi(x+L_x,y)&=\Psi(x,y),\\
\Psi(x,y+L_y)&=\Psi(x,y).\end{aligned}$ For a plane wave $e^{i(k_x x+k_y y)}$, these identifications require $k_x=\frac{2\pi n_x}{L_x},
\qquad
k_y=\frac{2\pi n_y}{L_y},
\qquad
n_x,n_y\in\mathbb Z.$ Both components of momentum are discrete.

zh: 反对易关系逆转了玻色子所呈现的统计行为。不存在全同费米子在同一模式中的受激堆积；该模式的占据会阻止另一个全同费米子进入其中。由于单个费米子态至多只能容纳一个全同费米子，因此把任意大量全同费米子放入该单一态并不能得到经典场极限。

p.src: Response: A bound composite containing an even number of fermionic constituents can have bosonic statistics. Putting several such composite bosons into the same overall state is not the same as putting their individual fermionic constituents into one identical single-particle state.

zh: 回答: 含有偶数个费米子组分的束缚复合体可以具有玻色统计。把若干个这样的复合玻色子放入同一个整体态，并不等同于把它们的各个费米子组分放入同一个全同单粒子态。

p.src: Composite statistics concern the bound object as a whole. Fermionic constituents can therefore combine into an object that behaves as a boson without violating exclusion for the constituents.

ja: 複合体の統計は、束縛された対象を全体として扱うものである。したがって、フェルミオン的構成要素は、構成要素に対する排他律に反することなく、ボソンとして振る舞う対象へと結合し得る。
zh: 复合粒子的统计性质关注的是作为整体的束缚客体。因此，费米子组分可以结合成一个表现为玻色子的客体，而不违反组分所服从的泡利不相容原理。

p.src: For the two descriptions to agree, the large-occupation state must be appropriately prepared and phase coherent; particle number alone is not sufficient. (The exchange supplies the many-quanta scale. Phase coherence is stated here as the additional condition that prevents large occupation alone from being mistaken for a classical field.)  In that semiclassical regime their effects agree up to small quantum deviations. This is a basic consistency condition. The electromagnetic field must describe discrete photons when individual quanta matter, yet an appropriately phase-coherent state containing many photons must reproduce the familiar action of a classical electromagnetic wave.

ja: 二つの記述が一致するには、大きな占有数の状態が適切に準備され、位相コヒーレントでなければならない。粒子数だけでは十分ではない。 (交換関係が多量子スケールを与える。位相コヒーレンスは、大きな占有数だけでは古典場と誤認されないための追加条件としてここで述べられている。)  その半古典的領域では、両者の効果は小さな量子的ずれを除いて一致する。これは基本的な整合性条件である。電磁場は、個々の量子が問題となる場合には離散的な光子を記述しなければならないが、多数の光子を含む適切に位相コヒーレントな状態は、古典電磁波のよく知られた作用を再現しなければならない。
zh: 要使这两种描述一致，大占据态必须被适当制备并且相位相干；仅靠粒子数并不足够。 (交换提供了多量子尺度。这里把相位相干表述为防止仅凭大占据就被误认为经典场的附加条件。)  在该半经典区域中，二者的效应在微小量子偏差范围内一致。这是一个基本的一致性条件。当单个量子起作用时，电磁场必须描述离散的光子；然而，一个适当相位相干且包含大量光子的态必须重现经典电磁波的熟悉作用。
